problem: Prior VLN agents (Seq2Seq/Student-forcing, RPA, Speaker-Follower) attend to the instruction but do not track which parts have been completed, which part comes next, or how far the agent is from the goal. The attention of the Speaker-Follower panoramic baseline, for example, grows diffuse later in an episode instead of moving forward through the instruction.
motivation: In VLN the agent has no explicit goal representation such as a map location or goal image. It can only infer its status by aligning the sequence of observations with the instruction. Boundaries between sub-instructions are soft, so the agent must keep both the completed and the upcoming parts grounded. Humans track progress toward goals in goal-directed behavior, and instructions are structurally aligned with trajectories: early words map to early steps. Together these suggest that the position of the instruction attention can be used as a progress signal.
key_idea: Couple visual-textual co-grounding with an auxiliary progress monitor. The monitor regresses normalized progress toward the goal from the textual attention distribution, which regularizes the grounding to move monotonically along the instruction. Its output is then reused at inference to score beam-search candidates or to trigger backtracking.
insight: Most of the gain comes from two sources. The first is architectural: grounding both text and vision from a shared LSTM state, and selecting actions with both h_t and the grounded instruction, lifts val-unseen SR from 27% (re-implemented Speaker-Follower panoramic baseline) to 42%. The second is using the progress estimate as a search heuristic. With greedy decoding the progress-monitor loss alone adds only about 2 SR on unseen (42→44), and progress-inference backtracking adds about 2 more (44→46). With beam search, adding the monitor raises val-unseen SR from 49 to 57 (Table 3, rows 6 vs 7), so beam search improves SR by 13 points with the monitor versus 7 without it. Speaker data augmentation adds only +1 SR on val-unseen with beam search (57→58), a much smaller boost than it gives Speaker-Follower; the authors read this as greater data efficiency. Attention plots show the textual grounding moving along a near-diagonal over time, while the baseline's attention becomes diffuse.
method: Instruction encoder: word embeddings (256-d, dropout 0.5) fed to an LSTM (512-d) give features X. Transformer-style positional encoding PE(x_l) is added before attention; max length is 80 words.

Panoramic visual input: for each navigable direction, a ResNet-152 feature (2048-d) is concatenated with the 4-d heading/elevation [sin φ, cos φ, sin θ, cos θ] tiled 32× (2176-d). An MLP g (BN→FC 1024→BN→Dropout→ReLU) projects it. Only navigable-direction images are used, not all 36 views.

Visual-textual co-grounding: the previous LSTM state h_{t-1} drives both textual soft-attention α_t over PE(X) and visual attention β_t over g(v_{t,k}). The decoder LSTM takes [x̂_t, v̂_t, a_{t-1}] to produce h_t, so text and vision are grounded from one shared state.

Action selection: each navigable direction is scored by the inner product (W_a[h_t, x̂_t])ᵀ g(v_{t,k}) and passed through a softmax. Training uses categorical sampling with a cross-entropy loss against the ground-truth next direction.

Progress monitor: an LSTM-like gate computes h^pm_t = σ(W_h[h_{t-1}, v̂_t]) ⊙ tanh(c_t). It predicts p^pm_t = tanh(W_pm[α_t, h^pm_t]), conditioned on the raw 80-d attention weights. It is trained with MSE toward normalized progress: 0 at start, 1 within 3 m of goal, and possibly negative if the agent moves farther away. Total loss is λ·CE + (1−λ)·MSE with λ=0.5.

Progress-aware inference: in state-factored beam search (beam 15, following Speaker-Follower), candidates are ranked by p^pm_t × p_{k,t}. Without beam search, 'progress inference' is greedy decoding that backtracks to the previous viewpoint and takes the next-best action whenever p^pm decreases.

setting.backbone: ImageNet ResNet-152 features (pre-extracted) + LSTM seq2seq encoder-decoder with co-grounding attention and progress-monitor head (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: R2R train split, plus in the * variants the exact same speaker-generated synthetic instructions as Speaker-Follower (size not stated in paper); supervised with ground-truth next direction and ground-truth distance-to-goal progress targets
setting.observation: panoramic RGB (ResNet-152 features of navigable directions + heading/elevation encoding)
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph viewpoints (panoramic action space: choose among navigable directions / stop)
setting.privileged: none (GT distance used only as training target); beam-search variants explore multiple candidate trajectories at test time (beam 15), and leaderboard submission logs all traversed viewpoints

numbers_note: All SR/OSR/SPL values are printed as fractions (e.g. 0.61) and are converted here to percent. TL is not reported. For beam search, the paper gives two test rows. The first computes OSR/SPL on the final selected trajectory. The second is leaderboard-compliant: all beam-traversed viewpoints are recorded, giving OSR 0.95–0.97 and SPL 0.02; later papers usually cite SPL 2 for Self-Monitoring (beam search). The arXiv LaTeX is a draft with leftover Overleaf notes, an ablation table marked 'To be removed' (baseline variants only), and a duplicated Table 3 in the appendix. Ablation rows (co-grounding only, PM with greedy decoding without augmentation, etc.) are in Tables 2 and 3 and are not listed individually here.
results: With beam search and speaker augmentation, the agent reaches 61% SR on R2R test-unseen versus 53% for Speaker-Follower* (+8, ranked #1 on the leaderboard at the time) and 58% SR / 52 SPL on val-unseen versus 55%. Without augmentation it still reaches 57% val-unseen SR versus Speaker-Follower's 50%. Without beam search, progress inference gives 48% test SR / 35 SPL versus 35% / 28 for Speaker-Follower* greedy, a 13-point gain. However, the leaderboard-compliant beam-search SPL is only 0.02.
limitations: Headline results depend on beam search (15 beams). Under leaderboard rules this produces extremely long trajectories (test SPL 0.02, OSR 0.97), so the method is impractical for a real single-run agent.

The progress monitor relies on the assumption that instruction order aligns monotonically with the trajectory, and it can be miscalibrated: in one failure case the agent strays but still reports high completeness. Progress-inference backtracking also adds path length.
Evaluated only on R2R in a discrete nav-graph with pre-extracted ResNet features. The paper does not test continuous environments, other datasets, or a real robot.
